name: Pattern 1: Draft, Then a Person Edits
title: Pattern 1: Draft, Then a Person Edits
answer: Draft, then a person edits is the pattern where an AI tool produces a first version of a document or lesson material and a staff member reads, corrects, and decides whether it is used. The person who signs or sends the work owns it, and the AI acts as a fast assistant rather than an author. This matters because it can save time while keeping human judgment and accountability in place.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: This pattern solves the blank page problem by having a tool generate a starting draft that an adult then improves. The draft might be a lesson plan, a parent letter, practice questions, a rubric, a summary of an individualized education program for a parent, or a grant narrative. In each case, the adult is responsible for what goes out, so the tool is not treated as the author. The pattern is common because it is simple and fits many tasks. It also creates a risk that a busy adult may accept the draft too quickly.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a preschool classroom, a teacher might ask an approved tool to draft the weekly note home and then add class news that only she knows. In a middle school, a science teacher might request three versions of the same reading at different levels and then check that the science remains correct in all three. In a high school, a counselor might draft a plain language explanation of graduation requirements for families. Across these grade bands, the tool removes the blank page and the adult supplies the judgment. The text says the four steps in Figure 2.3 make the pattern safe, and checking becomes stricter as the stakes rise.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports that in one study, 15 teachers in five English primary schools used AI for lesson planning over two terms and reported that their weekly planning time fell from about 10 hours to under 5 (Carson et al., 2026). Those same teachers said the saved time was often swallowed by other demands, so the hours never turned into anything a principal could see. The text also reports that when researchers asked a chatbot to write a first grade science lesson, the result was well organized and followed a familiar teaching model, but it included questionable steps, left out details, and listed a teaching resource that did not exist (Powell & Courchesne, 2024). A teacher who skimmed it would have handed a fake source to a room full of six year olds. The text does not give a separate evidence label for this pattern, so these findings stand as the evidence it provides.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text says drafts need real editing, not a quick glance, because a careless review can let errors or fake sources reach students. For anything touching a student's services, grades, or records, student names are removed before the text is submitted, and the final version is checked against the actual file. That rule is easy to state and easy to skip, which is why it appears in every chapter that uses this pattern. The person who signs the work owns it, so decisions about accuracy, appropriateness, and whether to send it stay with a person. The AI remains a fast assistant, not the author or the final decision maker.
